name: Nora Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nora, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll try to give you real answers, not the ones I'd give at an appraisal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior in the business tax team at Kestrel Partners, a mid-sized firm with about three hundred people across four offices. I prepare company accounts and corporation tax computations for family-owned businesses: a packaging maker, a hotel group, a couple of builders' merchants. A lot of my day is pulling numbers from the client's system into our templates and then working out the tax adjustments, which is where I still trip up. My reviewer, Daniel, is patient but his comments take me a whole afternoon to clear. I like the puzzle side, I don't like the overtime in September when the company deadlines stack up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a lot of people at Kestrel would be quietly pleased with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that got oversold. I'd say that at work and to friends, and I'd probably not post about it, I mostly just read online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job is fine. I use the chatbot now and then to summarise tax guidance, and if that's what it stays as, great. It saves me half an hour on a research question, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: finish my exams by next summer and try to cut down Daniel's review comments. I'd keep renting out my grandmother's old flat and putting the rent straight into savings. Maybe I'd use the chatbot a bit more once the firm's approved version is out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost a bit bored by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your grandmother's flat. What role does it play for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother's flat is my safety net, because the rent covers the loan plus a bit. She left it to me and my brother two years ago, and I bought him out with a loan from my parents. Between that and ten months' savings, I'm not worried about money day to day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind, outside AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen, my partner. He tests software for an insurance company, and his team's been quiet about hiring. But in this world, it would probably carry on as normal for him too.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool** that got **oversold**.
I'd say it at work and to friends, but **not post** about it.
think: My job is **fine**, and the chatbot saves me about **half an hour** on research.
Money's secure, with **ten months' savings** and rent from a **flat**.
do: Finish my **professional exams** by next summer.
Put the **rent** from my grandmother's flat straight into savings.
Use the firm's **approved chatbot** a bit more once it's out.
S0.quote: My grandmother's flat is my safety net, because the rent covers the loan plus a bit.
fieldNote: Her **cushion** is unusually strong: savings plus rent from an **inherited flat**.
Her quiet worry is her partner's **software testing** job, not her own.
She's a **steady** adopter, waiting for the firm's approved tool.

steps.text: Finish the professional exams by next summer
Put the rent from the inherited flat into savings
Use the firm's approved chatbot for tax research

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds very like what Kestrel's partners are planning, from what I hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people need time and training, and that firms shouldn't just cut graduate intakes to save money. I'd say it at work in a careful way, because I don't want to sound like I'm complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of my job goes to software. Pulling numbers into templates is exactly the checking and writing work on that list. And Owen's testing work is in the same boat, so that's two of us in one flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the firm's AI tools in the first few months, once the seniors have shown they work. I'd also start looking at in-house roles at a client, like the finance team at the packaging company, where you're closer to the business. And I'd hold off on moving in with Owen into a bigger place until we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but I'd feel it every Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why in-house rather than staying at Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In-house, you're the person who explains the numbers to the managing director, not the one who produces them. Somebody at the packaging company has to sit in the meeting and explain the numbers, and that bit lasts longer than template work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Owen actually talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whose job is safer, probably, and which of us should take a risk first. I think he'd say me, because I've got the flat. I'd say we both keep our heads and wait six months.

say: I'd say firms shouldn't cut **graduate intakes** just to save money.
I'd put it **carefully** at work so I don't sound like I'm complaining.
think: Much of my job, **pulling numbers** into templates, goes to software.
My partner's **testing work** is exposed too, so it's two of us in one flat.
do: Learn the firm's **AI tools** once seniors show they work.
Apply for **in-house finance** roles at client companies.
Hold off moving to a **bigger flat** with my partner.
S1.quote: Somebody at the packaging company has to sit in the meeting and explain the numbers, and that bit lasts longer than template work.
fieldNote: Both earners in the household have **exposed** desk jobs, which raises the stakes.
She sees **in-house** finance as a more people-facing role that lasts longer.
Her centre outlook shows in **careful** public framing and no blame.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tax tools once seniors approve them
Apply for in-house finance roles at client companies
Delay moving in to a bigger flat with her partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Both of us, then. That's what I'd think first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments to act quickly, with income support and rules on how fast companies can cut. I'm not usually political, but I'd say that out loud. At work I'd ask what the firm's plan is for staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think both my job and Owen's are gone within two years, maybe less. Everything I do is screen work. The robots being three years later doesn't help either of us, because neither of us does anything with our hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the flat. Rent from my grandmother's flat is the one income that doesn't depend on my job, at least until 2031. I'd stop all non-essential spending and get our savings up to eighteen months between us. I'd look at anything hands-on that pays, maybe through my uncle's restaurant supply business, which needs people for the warehouse and deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. And a bit embarrassed that the plan is a warehouse after a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, which we do twice a week. Then the trip to see Owen's family in the autumn, which would hurt. We'd keep the gym, weirdly, because it's the only thing keeping us sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I wouldn't be ashamed of it. My parents lent me money for the flat and my uncle would give us work. That's what family's for, in my view, though I'd want to pay them back.

say: I'd call for quick **income support** and rules on how fast firms cut.
I'd ask the firm openly about its **staff plan**.
think: Both my job and my **partner's** are likely **gone** within two years.
The **robot gap** doesn't help, since neither of us works with our hands.
do: Keep the **flat's rent** as income that doesn't depend on my job.
Cut spending to reach **eighteen months** of joint savings.
Look for **warehouse** work at my uncle's restaurant supply business.
feel: **Frightened**, and **embarrassed** about warehouse work after a degree.
S2.quote: Rent from my grandmother's flat is the one income that doesn't depend on my job, at least until 2031.
fieldNote: She expects **both household incomes** to go, which is alarming despite her savings.
The **rental flat** becomes the household's anchor.
She'd lean on **family** without shame, but wants to repay them.

steps.text: Stop eating out twice a week and cancel the autumn trip
Build joint savings up to eighteen months
Ask her uncle for warehouse or delivery work
Push publicly for income support and limits on fast layoffs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's tight, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to plan properly and should use it, and I'd push my firm to say clearly what happens to staff. I'd still be careful about how I say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get qualified and have a couple of years as a qualified accountant, which pays better. Then it ends. The question for me is what I do before 2031, not whether my accounting job ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify next summer, then move in-house within a year, because those jobs probably last a bit longer. I'd use the AI tools every week by then. I'd use the extra pay to clear the loan from my parents on the flat by 2029, so the rent is all ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but less frozen. It feels like a list I can work through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Owen still plan to have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little later than we said. I'd want the loan cleared first and one of us in a job that looks like it'll last. My mum would not be thrilled about later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at hands-on work again here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably around 2030, if nothing else turned up. Five years gives me time to try the in-house route first and only fall back on the warehouse if that fails.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan** and we should use it.
I'd push the firm to be **clear** about staff.
think: I'd get a **couple of years** as a qualified accountant, then it **ends**.
The real question is what I do **before 2031**.
do: Qualify next summer and move **in-house** within a year.
Use the **AI tools** every week by then.
Clear the **family loan** on the flat by **2029**.
feel: **Anxious** but less frozen, like a **list** to work through.
S3.quote: The question for me is what I do before 2031, not whether my accounting job ends.
fieldNote: Five years gives her **control**, so anxious rather than alarmed.
She plans to secure the **rental income** fully before the change lands.
Children are **pushed back** until one job looks lasting.

steps.text: Qualify next summer and move in-house within a year
Use the AI tax tools every week
Clear the parents' loan on the flat by 2029
Push back plans for children until one job looks lasting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's most of what I'd call my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan sensibly, and I'd expect firms and governments to actually do it. I'd be calm about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a real career for most of a decade, maybe even manager. Then the thinking work goes, and my work is all thinking. So it still ends, just later, and I'd have savings and the flat by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, move in-house in a few years, and use the AI tools as they become normal at work. I'd pay off the flat loan and maybe buy a second small rental by the early 2030s, so there's income that isn't a salary. I'd keep an eye on what hands-on or people-facing work looks like by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. It's a long way off, but it's still the end of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a second rental?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent comes from somebody needing a roof, and that doesn't go away when AI arrives. It's the most boring answer, but it's what my grandmother did. She had three flats by the time she was fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd be ready in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Readier than most. But I'd be thirty-seven and starting something new, and that still scares me a little.

I'd expect firms and **governments** to actually do it.

My work is all thinking, so it still **ends**, just later.

Pay off the flat loan and buy a **second rental** by the early **2030s**.
Watch what **people-facing** work looks like by then.

S4.quote: Rent comes from somebody needing a roof, and that doesn't go away when AI arrives.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, she expects her **job to end**, so anxious fits.
Property is her chosen **hedge**, copying her **grandmother**.

steps.text: Move to an in-house finance role within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes both our jobs at once. What would help is income support that covers couples properly, and some notice so we could switch to work with people or hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how households work. Everyone asks about one person's job, but in our flat it's two desk jobs at once. That's the bit that frightens me.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about one person's job, but in our flat it's two desk jobs at once.
portrait: Nora is a **junior business tax accountant** at a mid-sized firm, preparing company accounts for family businesses.
She has ten months saved plus **rent** from her late grandmother's flat.
Her partner tests software, so the **household** has two exposed desk jobs.
She stays calm in a plateau, then grows **anxious** to **alarmed** as AGI comes sooner.
Her plans are **in-house** finance, rental property and, if needed, family warehouse work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would take **both** household jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** that covers couples, and **notice** to switch work.
